learning_objective: Write and run your first SELECT query to return a customer contact list

end_state.visual_summary: Open the Execute SQL tab, type the commented query SELECT FirstName, LastName, Email FROM Customer, run it with F5, and show the result pane with the contact list

narration_beats.text: In this video, we will write our first SELECT query to pull a clean customer contact list for WSDA Music management. The goal is to return only the columns we need from the Customer table, so the result is focused and immediately useful.

DB Browser for SQLite shows the Browse Data view and the Execute SQL view. Browse Data displays raw table rows, while Execute SQL opens the SQL editor on top and an empty result pane below. The toolbar sits above the view area, and the editor is the large white area where we type.

observed_state.summary: DB Browser for SQLite is showing the Database Structure tab with a list of 11 tables and 10 indices for the wsda_music.db database.
observed_state.opening_state_log: [OPENING STATE] adapted: orientation summarized from actual screen

narration_beats.text: SELECT is the SQL command that chooses which columns to return, and FROM chooses which table holds those columns. Together they form the simplest useful query pattern: ask for specific data from one table. This keeps the result small and fast because the database does not waste time returning columns we do not need.

Right now the editor is empty and the result pane below it is blank. When we finish, the editor will hold a comment block followed by a formatted SELECT statement, and the result pane will show the customer contact list.

observed_state.summary: The Database Structure tab of the wsda_music.db SQLite database is displayed, showing a list of 11 tables and 10 indices with their schema definitions.

narration_beats.text: We type a comment header and the formatted query as one contiguous block in the SQL editor.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab shows a query selecting FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, with 60 rows returned and results displayed below.

narration_beats.text: We press F5 and the result pane fills with the contact list.

observed_state.summary: DB Browser for SQLite showing the Execute SQL tab with a query selecting FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, displaying 60 returned rows in the results grid below.

narration_beats.text: We see 60 rows returned with FirstName, LastName, and Email for each customer, confirming the contact list is complete and the query ran exactly as intended.

observed_state.summary: The Execute SQL tab shows a query selecting FirstName, LastName, and Email from the Customer table, with results displayed below and a success message indicating 60 rows returned in 15ms.

narration_beats.text: The result pane shows the complete customer contact list, with each customer record appearing exactly once in the order it is stored. Management now has a reliable set of first names, last names, and email addresses without extra columns cluttering the view. Because the database returned only the columns we requested, the output is compact and fast to scan.

Adding a comment header at the top of the query is a professional habit. It records who created the query, when it was written, and what problem it solves, which helps anyone who opens the file later. Good comments turn a quick one-off query into documentation that the whole team can trust and maintain.

We have written our first SELECT query and pulled a complete customer contact list. The query returned only the columns we needed and included a clear comment header. Next, we will make those column headers friendlier for management reports by using aliases.
